replying_to: Replying to Generating Landmark Navigation Instructions from Maps as a Graph-to-Text Problem

content.title: Needs Improvement
content.review:
[Summary]

This paper presents the task of generating landmark-based navigation instructions given a graph representing a path on a map. The authors collect ~8K instructions by having AMT workers annotate maps with censored street names — forcing workers to rely on landmark entities (e.g., starbucks). Their experiments employ a (graph) encoder (text) decoder transformer. Both human- and model-generated instructions are evaluated via BLEU score and human navigation success (collected via AMT).

[Pros]

This paper is very well written and easy to follow. In particular, documenting how the data were collected and prepared. I thought the figures being used were very effective. The notation used in the modeling section was also very clearly structured, and I didn’t find myself needing to scan back for previously defined notation.

It’s also great to see human evaluations included in the results!

[Cons]

Motivation:

My key issue with this paper is that the motivation isn’t very clear to me. The introduction makes three cases: (1) humans efficiently navigate via landmarks in the instructions, (2) inexact GPS tracking and imperfect human distance judgements, and (3) landmarks are more visually salient than street signs — and are thus better for bikers/bus riders.

(1) It’s true that people anchor to visually salient landmarks, however the landmarks present on the map (and thus mentioned by the AMT workers) don’t necessarily correlate to visual saliency.

(2) While inexact GPS tracking breaks distance based instructions, streets and intersections can still form a graph from which instructions can be generated.

(3) See my point on (1).

Data and modeling:

The author mentions that one of the failure modes during annotation is when workers mix up left/right — which you’d expect, as they’re generating egocentric instructions given an allocentric perspective. This again ties back to point (1), which is to say that landmarks from an allocentric perspective may not correspond to what’s salient from an egocentric perspective. And while the model itself is clear, simple, and well-suited for the task, the model’s capacity seems overkill for the relatively small dataset (~8K instructions).

Experiments and evaluation:

I’m very happy that the reviewers included human evaluations for their model predictions — as language generation tasks too often rely on automatic metrics, such as BLEU.

However, my biggest concern is that there are no simple baselines to compare the model’s performance to. Given that this paper presents a new task, it would be beneficial to see results for a trivial rule-based systems, like the one used to generate the 20K pretraining data. Likewise, some ablation experiments, such as: corrupting the graph structure, reordering landmarks, only including the final landmark etc.

Finally, for the human evaluations, in addition to reporting Success Rate (SR) and Edit Distance (ED), the authors ought to look into more recent evaluation metrics for navigation, such as Success weighted by Path Length (SPL) and Normalized Dynamic Time Warping (nDTW).

[Clarifying Questions]

Does ang(u, v) encode an angle in a global coordinate system or relative to the angle of the previous edge?

[Additional Feedback]

N/A
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection
content.confidence: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature

content.title: Reply to AnonReviewer2
content.comment:
Thank you for your valuable comments.

##### Motivation:
Visual saliency of landmarks: The **landmarks in our dataset are in fact visually salient** due to the validation of each human-generated natural language instruction by another human who has to follow the instruction using Google Street View. Instructions that contain landmarks that are only visible on the map but not in Street View (like buildings with no visible name tag) did not lead to successful validation and were discarded from the dataset. Further, instructions writers knew about the mode of evaluation and thus chose types of landmarks that are likely visible in Street View / real life.

Inexact GPS information: Our motivational comment was meant to address inexactness of GPS information on the side of the GPS system (poor signal) and on the side of the human user (street sign might be occluded or not readable for bus/bike riders). In neither case it is possible or useful to generate instructions from a street graph.

##### Data and modeling:
Egocentric vs. allocentric perspective: Although the instructions writers did not see the route in first person perspective, in our setting **objects are in fact referenced to in egocentric manner**. This is because the annotator is given a starting and goal direction and thus knows the facing direction for the rest of the route. Furthermore, we added a linguistic analysis of 25 randomly sample navigation instructions, comparing our data to Room-to-Room and Touchdown (Table 2), showing the largest number of egocentric spatial relationships in our dataset. Lastly the human validation by Street View adds a clearly egocentric perspective to the data annotation.

Baselines: We **added two baselines** together with a manual evaluation by human navigation using Street View on 200 examples and the suggested evaluation metric of nDTW (Table 3). We compare a rule-based system (stringing together all POIs and intersection along the route, where intersections are followed by turning directions), a seq2seq system (trained to generate natural language instructions from the rule-based outputs), and an enhanced graph2text system (adding a copy mechanism) with and without pretraining on rule-based instructions. The results show that the instructions generated by the rule-based system are exact by including all possible landmarks, thus they yield a high success rate, but they do not resemble natural language (low BLEU) and are hard to read (highest time penalty). The learned systems are improved by adding graphs and pretraining, yielding the same success rate on partially seen test data as rule-based at a much reduced time penalty, and coming close on unseen test data.

##### Clarifying question:
ang(u,v) is relative to route directions, i.e., relative to the previous edge, making the representation rotation invariant.


Edit:
We included a section in the appendix that discusses reasons for failed navigation runs and shows that orientation mistakes in the instructions are filtered out by the navigation run validation.

content.title: lacking in dataset comparison and model error analysis
content.review:
The authors of this paper construct a new dataset for generating route instructions in natural language from maps (OpenStreetMaps) and promises to release the dataset upon publication.  The authors consider road networks to be a graph, and proposes the task of generating natural language landmark route instruction from this graph.  As a baseline for the task, they also propose a deep learning based model that takes a graph and produces route instructions.   
The paper is a resource paper and at the same time engineering paper that establish a baseline for a new task.  

Pros:
+ Compared with previous datasets of similar kind, the constructed dataset is a bit larger and based on street maps (instead of virtual office environments).
+ A sophisticated baseline model, what seems to be a state of the art graph to sequence model, is evaluated in the experiments. 

Cons:
- As a resource paper, this paper is a bit light on comparing proposed dataset  with older datasets.  
- A bit light on dataset analysis.  What were the causes of requiring second try in navigation run task?  
-  It's not clear what authors did with slightly wrong instructions or ones that mixes up left and right and so on.  
- There is only one baseline in the experiment.   This reader suspect that a simple hand crafted heuristic can have easily 50% or more SR@25 considering the results in Cercas Curry et al.
- Graph to sequence model is nice to have,  but it is a complex model with a lot of tuning point.   It also requires more training data and it would be tough to train it with few thousands.  Careful analysis is required to see if it reached its full potential. 

Please take a look at NLP engineering experiment paper and resource paper section of the following site: https://coling2018.org/paper-types/  and answer every question to improve the paper.  

Overall, the paper seems to address everything minimally required, but its treatment of the problem is not thorough.  
Due to its lack of dataset comparison and error analysis, I vote for marginally below acceptance.
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Reply to AnonReviewer3
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive comments, please find our response below.

##### Comparison of datasets:
In the new version of the paper we **include two types of comparisons to older datasets**. We present a table with statistics about the number of instances, route types and instruction length. We also conduct a qualitative linguistic analysis by quantifying relevant phenomena in our instructions compared to other data sets.

##### Instruction validation:
The instructions that were not validated during data collection are not included in the dataset. A second try in the navigation run task was performed if the first annotator didn’t stop within the 25 meter radius around the goal location. This can have various reasons ranging from bad instructions, distracted annotators or technical problems on the annotators side. 

##### Baselines:
We now include **two baselines in our experiments**. One is a heuristic “rule based” system. Unfortunately, to our knowledge, the systems presented in Cercas Curry et al or similar papers are not available (anymore?).

display_title: proposed model not significantly better than simple rule based baseline

content.title: proposed model not significantly better than simple rule based baseline
content.comment:
OK, the baseline is added now.  But the proposed model is not performing significantly better than a simple heuristic.
I suspect that the proposed model is overfitting.  There would be no point of proposing a complex system if it does not outperform a simple baseline.   Authors should compare the outputs of each system and see which examples the heuristic is doing better.   That should give us insights into how to improve the proposed system.  Then come up with a feature that can be incorporated to the proposed system so that it does not overfit.  Clearly state the insights in the paper.  At this point, the proposed model is inferior and the error analysis is still not done yet.

content.title: Reply to AnonReviewer3
content.comment: We do not agree with the assessment that the baseline is doing better (or equally good) at the considered task of generating Natural Language Landmark Navigation Instructions. The rule based baseline is clearly not emitting natural language, but measures the navigation success rate when all available route information is extracted with a heuristic and put into text form. The seq2seq baseline is trained to generate natural language from the rule based text. Qualitative analysis shows that it succeeds in generating natural language output, but fails when evaluating for navigation success. Only the proposed graph based method succeeds at both tasks simultaneously - generating natural language while achieving good navigation performance. We use early stopping on the dev set to prevent overfitting. If overfitting on the training set would be a solution for the task, the seq2seq model should show similar performance as the graph-to-text model. Also the diverse outputs from the learned systems in Figure 4 indicate that there is no memorization. We will include further examples from all systems in the appendix and also analyse the properties of routes that failed for each system.

content.title: Making the dataset publicly available is expected.
content.review:
The paper describes an approach to a natural language instruction system for route navigation. 
The system encodes a route on a map into a location- and rotation-invariant graph representation, and from the representation, natural language instructions are generated.
The main contribution of this paper seems to be two-fold. The authors created a dataset for Natural Language Landmark Navigation Instructions (NLLNI) using crowdsourcing. They developed a method for NLLNI. The performance of the system is evaluated through an experiment.


NLLNI task is still an important and challenging task. The authors tackle the problem of combining map-to-graph representation and graph-to-text architecture by preparing their original data. The method itself seems interesting.

However, both contributions have some limitations.

The proposed method is only compared to the reference in evaluation, as table 1 shows. As the authors mentioned, at least we have rule-based methods and other naive methods for NLLNI. The performance of the proposed method should be compared to such a pre-existing method for evaluation. Therefore, it is difficult to judge if the method is working appropriately.

Though the paper exaggerates the importance of the novel dataset, they are not providing it as an open dataset to my understanding. If so, that cannot be the contribution to the community. 

If the authors add several baseline methods to Table 1 and provide the novel dataset as an open dataset, I think this paper becomes a more valuable paper. 

---------------------

Because of the improvement and the clarification in the revised manuscript, I have changed the rating after the rebuttal.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Reply to AnonReviewer1
content.comment:
Thank you for the insightful comments which are helpful for us to improve our work.

##### Baselines:
In the new version of the paper we compare our model with **two additional baselines**. First we show evaluation results on the “rule based” system that was used to pretrain the model. Second we train a sequence-to-sequence model to generate natural language instructions from the rule based sequences. 

##### Dataset release:
There has been a misunderstanding: **We will of course release our full dataset!**
We stated in section 3.4. of the submitted paper that we will release the dataset including the preprocessed route representations and collected navigation instructions. This allows to reproduce and improve results on the task. As noted by another reviewer, the dataset will also be valuable for the reverse task of training a visual agent to follow natural language instructions.

display_title: Interesting work but limited novelty and results are not promising. However, data released might be valuable and overall the methodology and problem formulation is nicely implemented.

content.title: Interesting work but limited novelty and results are not promising. However, data released might be valuable and overall the methodology and problem formulation is nicely implemented.
content.review:
Summary:

This paper presents a graph-to-text transformer model to generate navigational instructions from graph-based OpenStreetMap inputs, by conditioning on salient landmarks existing in the graph of the map + supervised by human instructions---a new dataset of navigation instructions to be released with this work. They empirically evaluate the quality of the generated instructions based on their score in comparison to human-generated instructions for the same samples, as well as how well they could be used to lead a human to navigate in Street View, given the model-generated utterance. 


Reason for score:

I thought this paper approached an interesting problem (generate instructions in a navigation domain) based on a graph representation of a street map. However, I think the results are not up to par and moreover, there isn’t a novel modelling approach (graph transformers have been used widely so far)---and I think a different way might lead to improved performance that would benefit this paper. The analysis is also somewhat lacking (e.g., it would be good to see failure cases of models to understand why the performance is so low and what could help overcome this) and also a simple baseline based on an object-oriented trajectory would be helpful to have as well. 


Positive points + questions:

1. The example/qualitative analysis of generated instructions in the figure looks great! However this does not align with the empirical evaluations that show quite poor performance---it would be good to show a larger range of examples (instead of just one) as well as some analysis of failure cases that lead to poor performance, and in what aspects the model generation suffers.

2. The data released with this paper is valuable for a range of instruction-following tasks. It would be good to have a better analysis of the language and instructions to understand the linguistic phenomena that this dataset includes.

3. It would also be good to compare this to existing datasets in OSM that have instructions and existing navigation instructions in general, to get a sense of how these instructions fare in comparison to others in the domain. Example, these dataset papers have nice comparisons---and should be cited given the similarities! (https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.07954 and https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.12354.pdf)

4. While the modelling/graph-to-text setup is sound and makes sense, it would be interesting to see if having more state information for each node (e.g., even making it more real and image-based) helps performance.


Negative points + questions:

1. How well do other instruction-generation baselines work? For e.g., one possibility is a simple supervised seq2seq that doesn’t take in the graph structure and is supervised by the human instructions in the dataset.

2. ^for example, previous work linked below, attempts to have a generation model that takes in the route/graph of the environment as a sequence of nodes, and attempts to generate natural language instructions by performing a greedy prediction over word tokens, supervised by human instructions. Since all of these components exist here (e.g., graph, route, instruction supervision) this is a natural baseline to implement and compare to.

3. Another important baseline is a model that does have access to a graph structure and is based on a simple grammar (e.g., CFG-like) and the object-oriented trajectory from the graph route. (this would likely have instructions that are rigid/inflexible/less novel words therefore potentially lower BLEU scores, but would have higher instruction-following results for the human experiments) so an analysis along those axes of evaluation metrics would be interesting to see.

4. Missing reference for speaker-listener generation for instructions: https://papers.nips.cc/paper/7592-speaker-follower-models-for-vision-and-language-navigation.pdf
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Reply to AnonReviewer4
content.comment:
We want to thank the reviewer for the valuable suggestions!
##### Comparison of datasets:
 The new version has a **qualitative analysis of linguistic phenomena present in our instructions and compares it to other data sets**. Besides the linguistic analysis we also included a table with statistics of multiple navigation instructions data sets. The suggested references are now cited. We will include many more examples in the appendix and discuss shortcomings of the generated instructions in the results section. 
##### Baselines:
In the new version we **included two baselines**. First we evaluate on the “rule based” instructions that are also used to pretrain the model. Second, we train a sequence-to-sequence model that takes the rule based instructions as input and is learned to generate the natural language instructions. The rule based sequences can be seen as a linearization of the route representation. 

Key motivation of the work as stated in the title is to generate navigation instructions from maps. This has the advantage of global coverage and more up to date information than say Street View images. However, it would be an interesting experiment to enhance nodes with panoramas from a previous date and evaluate instructions in an up-to-date environment. This would reflect the real world setting of having up-to-date map data and out-of-date Street View images. We see this as future research directions but not in the scope of this work.

display_title: Overview over improvements in updated version: baselines, dataset comparisons, architecture updates

content.title: Overview over improvements in updated version: baselines, dataset comparisons, architecture updates
content.comment:
We want to thank all reviewers for their helpful comments and suggestions.
##### Baselines:
One main concern was the lack of baselines in the experiment section. In the updated version of the paper we included **two additional baselines** and the graph-to-text model without pretraining. The first baseline is a heuristic **rule based system** that strings together all POIs and intersections along the route. For each intersection the correct direction is indicated. The second baseline is a **sequence-to-sequence model** that uses the rule based instructions as input and is trained to produce the corresponding natural language instructions. 
##### Comparison of datasets:
Another critique is the insufficient comparison to existing data sets. We now included a **qualitative analysis of linguistic phenomena present in our instructions and compares it to other data sets** and a table with metrics about number of instances, route types and instruction length of existing datasets. 
##### Other:
The results section now includes a discussion about the generated instructions and possible shortcomings. We also improved the presented graph-to-model by integrating copy mechanism which yield better results, especially on the unseen test set. Further we changed the attention mechanism to be exactly in line with the Graph Attention Network architecture.
